clue.text: Cat's-cradle in America?

parts.note: a 'cat' is a jazz musician, so the cradle of cats is the birthplace of jazz, a city in Louisiana

explanation.walkthrough: The string game cat's-cradle is a red herring: read 'cat' as jazz slang for a player and 'cradle' as birthplace.
explanation.definitionFit: The Louisiana city is widely called the cradle or birthplace of jazz, whose players are nicknamed cats.

clue.text: Knot done badly

indicators.note: done badly suggests the letters of the word are put together wrongly

explanation.surface: Someone's knot has been tied poorly.
explanation.definitionFit: A node is a knot or lump, as on a plant stem or in a tied line.

clue.text: Beaufort's atomic plant?

explanation.walkthrough: Windscale was the old name of the Sellafield nuclear site in Cumbria, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Admiral Beaufort devised a scale for rating wind force, and the Cumbrian nuclear works was formerly named after that same word pair.

clue.text: Dance from Burma? No!

indicators.note: the exclamation says the country's name is not right as it stands, so its letters must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A dance that comes from Burma? Certainly not!
explanation.walkthrough: 'No!' is the anagram signal: the dance is not from Burma, but its letters are.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumba is a Cuban ballroom dance.

clue.text: Need gag perhaps for such telephone lines

definitions.note: describes the state of a busy line, an adjective

indicators.note: perhaps hints the words need gag are one possible arrangement of the letters wanted

explanation.surface: Busy phone lines may need a gag to silence them.
explanation.definitionFit: A line that is busy, with a call already in progress, is said to be engaged.

clue.text: Frank brought up with twitch, favouring the family

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means the word is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: frank means open, candid
a tic is a nervous twitch

explanation.surface: Frank, raised with a nervous twitch, always favours his relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' turns OPEN to NEPO; 'Frank' looks like a man's name but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Nepotism is favouritism shown to relatives, and this adjective describes it.

clue.text: Driver, perhaps, in a black suit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Driver' suggests a motorist; it is the golf stick used off the tee.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver is one kind of golf stick, and in a pack of cards clubs is one of the two dark suits.

clue.text: A blockhead in retirement ki became a cleaner in Bath

indicators.note: retiring means going backwards, so the words are read in reverse

parts.note: a blockhead is a fool

explanation.surface: A dimwit who retired became a cleaner in the spa town of Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retirement' turns A FOOL into the bath sponge; Bath, the English spa town, is a lower-case bath in disguise. The 'ki' in the held clue is stray OCR.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofah is a dried gourd sponge used for scrubbing in the bathtub.

clue.text: Late — how one smothers laugh!

explanation.definitionFit: Behindhand means overdue or running late, and stifling a giggle means putting one's palm over the mouth.

clue.text: Obscure way Bert's yet to Ta find it

annotationWithheld.why: Held as 'Obscure way Bert's yet to Ta find it': BERT'S YET gives the letters, but the anagram indicator is garbled ('to Ta find it') and the original could not be found.
annotationWithheld.clue: Obscure way Bert's yet to Ta find it

clue.text: Blue material dug up and put back

indicators.note: put back means the word is turned round and written backwards

parts.note: dug up, as ore from a pit, means mined

explanation.surface: Blue cloth excavated and then returned to its place.
explanation.definitionFit: Denim is the sturdy cotton twill, usually indigo-dyed, used for jeans.

clue.text: Delicate craft of Chichester

parts.note: Sir Francis Chichester flew a de Havilland light aircraft and sailed a yacht of this name; the name is also a fragile insect

explanation.walkthrough: Francis Chichester was the English aviator and sailor who sailed solo round the world in 1966-67.
explanation.definitionFit: Chichester's plane and yacht both bore the name of the light moth that inspired the aircraft range.

clue.text: This slow-mover is French is French, carrying freight

indicators.note: carrying means the first word holds the second within it

parts.note: est is French for is
cargo is freight

explanation.surface: A slow creature that is French, burdened with freight.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue repeats 'is French' through an OCR slip; once only is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: An escargot is an edible snail, a famously slow creature.

clue.text: Mark's old couple

explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Clemens wrote under the pen name Mark Twain, and twain is an archaic word for two.

clue.text: Lines on young child is giving chest trouble

parts.note: BR is British Rail, the railway lines
a chit is a young child

explanation.surface: Lines laid on a little one give her a bad chest.
explanation.definitionFit: Bronchitis is inflammation of the airways in the lungs, a chest illness.

clue.text: Succeeded in getting awkward header round Chelsea's No. 1

indicators.note: round means the jumbled letters go about the other piece
an awkward header is a clumsy one, so its letters are rearranged
number one is the first letter of the team name

explanation.surface: A footballer scores with a clumsy header for Chelsea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' scrambles HEADER, which goes 'round' C, the first letter of Chelsea, a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: To have reached something is to have managed to get to it.

clue.text: Wednesday's break from work?

parts.note: Wednesday is midway through the week, and a pause halfway through a match is the interval

explanation.definitionFit: The interval halfway through a game is a rest; Wednesday sits at the midpoint of the week.

clue.text: Nurse displaying rare riches at hospital

indicators.note: rare as in unusual or undercooked, the letters are set in a new order

parts.note: H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A nurse shows off unusual wealth at the hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurse' is a verb here: to nurse a hope is to keep it dear.
explanation.definitionFit: To nurse a feeling or hope is to hold it dear.

clue.text: Unyielding, yet am mobile about five, oddly

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go around the other piece
oddly suggests the letters are arranged in a strange order

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral five

explanation.surface: Stubborn, though I am mobile around five o'clock, strangely.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unyielding is fixed and cannot be shifted.

clue.text: Isle of Wight's sewers, practically unnecessary

indicators.note: practically means almost all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: needless means unnecessary

explanation.surface: The Isle of Wight's drainage is almost redundant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sewers' is not drains but people or tools that sew. The Needles are chalk stacks off the Isle of Wight, England, so that phrase is extra flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that sew, the pointed tools that stitch, are sewers in the sense of stitchers.

clue.text: One staying out is feared by net savers

explanation.definitionFit: A worker who walks out in a dispute is on strike, and a goalkeeper guarding the net fears the forward who shoots.

clue.text: Pitch of the roof?

parts.note: pitch here is the black tarry substance used for covering roofs, not the slope

explanation.definitionFit: Bitumen is a tarry mineral pitch used for waterproofing roofs and roads.

clue.text: Sword-belt for ribald sort taking a lot on

indicators.note: to sort is to rearrange, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a lot

explanation.surface: A sword-belt for a bawdy fellow who takes on a great deal.
explanation.definitionFit: A baldric is a belt worn over the shoulder to carry a sword.

clue.text: Outward appearance of brother …

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs into 24-across, but each clue stands alone; 'brother' is a monk.
explanation.definitionFit: Habit can mean bearing or outward look, and it is the robe worn by a monk or friar.

clue.text: It needs pluck to put curse si on little woman

parts.note: to ban is to curse or proscribe
Jo is the March sister in Little Women

explanation.surface: It takes courage to swear at a small woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pluck' means courage on the surface but plucking strings in the definition. The 'si' in the held clue is stray OCR.
explanation.definitionFit: A banjo is a stringed instrument played by plucking.

clue.text: … brother is one corresponding

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links it to 22-across for the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: A sibling is a family member, and relative also means proportionate or comparable.

clue.text: If the order is not the usual, he'll help himself

indicators.note: the letters are said to be out of their normal order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: If things are out of order, he will take what he wants.
explanation.definitionFit: A robber helps himself to what belongs to others.

clue.text: Shift one makes for oneself has feminine finish

parts.note: F is the grammar abbreviation for feminine
end means finish

explanation.surface: A woman's survival effort ends on a feminine note.
explanation.definitionFit: To fend for oneself is to make shift, managing without help.

clue.text: Camp producer?

parts.note: camp read as a set of canvas shelters, so someone who makes them, not a theatrical producer of camp shows

explanation.definitionFit: St Paul's trade was making tents, the shelters of a camp.

clue.text: Inspire some slim Buenos Aires characters

indicators.note: some of the letters, with characters, means a run is taken from inside the words

explanation.surface: Inspire a few slender people from the Argentine capital.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbue is to fill or permeate with a feeling or idea.

clue.text: Cocaine spoiling TV picture?

explanation.definitionFit: Coke is slang-named after white flakes, and interference speckling a screen looks like falling white flakes.

clue.text: Are only refractory people employed here? No, it's good fellows' ground

definitions.text: Are only refractory people employed here?

parts.note: a brick is a good, reliable fellow; the plural possessive joins it to the next word
a field is a ground

explanation.surface: A workplace staffed only by stubborn people? No, a pitch for fine chaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refractory' means stubborn of people, but heat-resistant of bricks.
explanation.definitionFit: A brickworks is where heat-resistant clay blocks are made.
